title: Heat stress challenges in marathon vs. ultra-endurance running
authors: Bouscaren N, Millet GY, Racinais S
journal: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
population: Conceptual comparison of heat-stress risk factors in marathon vs ultra-endurance (events longer than 6 h) running
findings: Studies on exercise longer than a marathon in the heat are sparse, so marathon knowledge cannot be transposed to ultra-endurance events (>6 h; variable distance, elevation, technicality, altitude, night running).

Marathon-specific heat risks: high running intensity (especially for the fastest runners), urban high-albedo surfaces and a hot self-generated microclimate in mass-participation events (for average to slow runners).

Ultra-specific heat risks: uphill running or walking (sometimes with poles), long-haul travel to exotic destinations, desert environments, and the need to sustain thermoregulatory and sweating responses for several days.
Authors call for specific research on hot conditions in ultra-endurance disciplines.
limitations: Narrative, opinion-level, no quantitative estimates; explicitly states ultra evidence is lacking.
implications: Do not reuse marathon heat-penalty values for events above 6 h without a flag; give ultra heat adjustments a lower-confidence label.
Adjust heat factors by event profile (climbs, night, multi-day, travel) rather than one global coefficient; no numeric values are justified.
Treat long-haul travel to a hot or desert venue as a trigger for an early acclimation block.

verification.notes: Crossref (Front Sports Act Living 2019-11-13) and Europe PMC abstract re-fetched; all statements match.
